**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties** | Property | Value / Description | |----------|---------------------| | **Atomic number** | 1 | | **Atomic mass** | 1.008 u (average; 1.00794 u for ^1H) | | **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | | **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | | **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | | **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | | **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | | **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 g cm⁻³) | | **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | | **Molecular weight (H₂)** | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ | | **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 432 kJ mol⁻¹ | | **Dipole moment** | 0 (homonuclear diatomic) | | **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series (UV/visible/IR) | | **Reactivity** | Highly flammable; reacts with O₂, N₂, halogens, acids, metals (forming hydrides). | | **Oxidation states** | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (molecular H₂). | | **Acidity/basicity** | Weak acid (HF) when bonded to electronegative atoms; hydride (H⁻) is a strong base. | | **Isotopes** | • **^1H (protium)** – most abundant (99.98%)
• **^2H (deuterium)** – stable, 0.015%
• **^3H (tritium)** – radioactive, half‑life ≈12.32 y | | **Physical state at room temperature** | Gas (diatomic H₂) | | **Solubility in water** | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | | **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 28.84 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) | | **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) | | **Electrical conductivity** | Very low in neutral form; high in plasma or ionized state. | | **Flammability limits** | Lower explosive limit (LEL): 4 % vol; Upper explosive limit (UEL): 75 % vol in air. | | **Miscellaneous** | Forms hydrogen bonds in compounds like water (H₂O) and ammonia (NH₃); participates in proton transfer reactions; used as a reducing agent (e.g., in hydrogenation). | --- ### Quick Takeaways - **Lightest element**: Atomic mass ≈1 u; extremely low density. - **Highly reactive**: Forms hydrides with metals, reacts violently with oxygen, and is a powerful reducing agent. - **Isotopic diversity**: Protium (^1H) is the most common; deuterium and tritium have nuclear applications (e.g., fusion research). - **Key role in chemistry & physics**: Basis for the periodic table, essential in stellar nucleosynthesis, and a primary fuel source in hydrogen‑fuel cells.
